title: The Tale of a Tiny Link

scenes.title: Meet the cast
scenes.narration: Snip turns long web addresses into tiny ones. Our hero is one long link that is about to become snip.dev/Ab3x9Qz. First, meet the places it will visit.

nodes.label: You
nodes.step: You have a long link to share and not much room to share it.

nodes.label: web/Shorten.tsx
nodes.step: You paste it into the Shorten box and press the button.
nodes.details: A small React form. It sends the long URL to the API and shows the short link that comes back, with a copy button.

nodes.label: src/server.ts
nodes.step: The API server is the front desk: it makes short links and sends visitors on their way.
nodes.details: An Express app with two routes that matter: POST /links makes a short link, GET /:code redirects a visitor. A rate limiter sits in front of both.
nodes.code:
app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 60_000, max: 30 }))
app.post('/links', createLink)
app.get('/:code', followLink)

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.step: Redis is the quick memory: it remembers popular links so most visits never touch the database.
nodes.details: Keys look like link:Ab3x9Qz and hold the long URL, kept for 24 hours. Also holds a list of clicks waiting to be counted.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.step: Postgres is the record book: every link ever made, and how often it was clicked.
nodes.details: One table, links(code, url, created_at, clicks). code is the primary key, so two links can never share a code.

points: Fast path: Redis. Source of truth: Postgres. If they ever disagree, Postgres wins.

scenes.title: Making a short link
scenes.narration: Our long link knocks on the front desk. Before it gets a short name, two guards check it over.

nodes.label: POST /links
nodes.step: The request arrives with the long URL in its body.

nodes.label: rateLimit()
nodes.step: Guard 1, the rate limiter: more than 30 requests a minute from one address? Come back later.
nodes.details: Counts requests per IP in Redis with a one-minute window, so it works even with several server instances.

nodes.label: isValidUrl()
nodes.step: Guard 2 checks it is a real http or https address, and not a link to Snip itself.
nodes.code:
const u = new URL(raw)
if (!['http:', 'https:'].includes(u.protocol)) return false
if (u.hostname === 'snip.dev') return false   // no loops
return true

nodes.label: makeCode()
nodes.step: makeCode() invents a short name: 7 random letters and digits, like Ab3x9Qz.
nodes.details: 62 possible characters in 7 places is about 3.5 trillion names, so a clash is rare. When one happens, the database refuses it and makeCode() simply tries again.

nodes.label: insertLink()
nodes.step: insertLink() writes code and URL into Postgres.

nodes.label: 201 + short link
nodes.step: 201 Created: the form shows snip.dev/Ab3x9Qz with a copy button. Our hero has its new name.

nodes.label: 429 slow down
nodes.step: Too many requests: a 429 answer, and the form asks you to wait a minute.

nodes.label: 400 bad URL
nodes.step: Not a real web address: a 400 answer explaining why.

points: Both guards run before any database write, so junk never reaches Postgres.
A code clash is not an error you see: makeCode() just rolls again.

scenes.title: Following a short link
scenes.narration: Days later, a friend clicks snip.dev/Ab3x9Qz. This is the busy part of Snip, so it is built to be fast.

nodes.label: GET /Ab3x9Qz
nodes.step: A friend clicks the short link.

nodes.label: in Redis?
nodes.step: First question: does the quick memory already know this code?
nodes.code:
const cached = await redis.get(`link:${code}`)
if (cached) return res.redirect(302, cached)

nodes.label: 302 redirect
nodes.step: Cache hit: a 302 redirect sends the browser on to the long URL. No database needed.

nodes.label: findLink()
nodes.step: Cache miss: ask the record book, Postgres.

nodes.label: cache it
nodes.step: Found: copy it into Redis for 24 hours, so the next click is quick, then redirect.

nodes.label: 404 page
nodes.step: Not in Postgres either: a friendly 404 page.

nodes.label: count click
nodes.step: Either way, the click is dropped into a waiting list in Redis to be counted later.

points: Most clicks end at Redis: the database only sees the first click after a link drops out of the cache.
Counting a click never slows the redirect: it is only written to a list.

scenes.title: Counting clicks
scenes.narration: Writing to the database on every click would be slow. So a small night-shift worker counts them in batches.

nodes.label: clicks list
nodes.step: Clicks pile up in a Redis list: just a code per click.

nodes.label: jobs/clicks.ts
nodes.step: Every 10 seconds the click job wakes up and takes up to 1,000 of them.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.step: It adds them up per code and writes one UPDATE per link, not one per click.

nodes.label: Stats page
nodes.step: The stats page reads the totals, a few seconds behind real time, and nobody minds.

points: Gotcha: if the server stops mid-batch, those clicks are lost. Fine for stats, not for money.

scenes.title: Where to start reading
scenes.narration: Now you know the story. Read the code in the order our link travelled.

nodes.label: src/server.ts
nodes.step: src/server.ts: the routes and the rate limiter, in 30 lines.

nodes.label: routes/links.ts
nodes.step: src/routes/links.ts: createLink() and followLink(), the two journeys.

nodes.label: lib/cache.ts
nodes.step: src/lib/cache.ts: the Redis side.

nodes.label: jobs/clicks.ts
nodes.step: src/jobs/clicks.ts: the click counter.

points: Gotcha: deleting a link in Postgres leaves it working for up to 24 hours until its Redis copy expires.
